paper_a.title: An Elementary Proof of a Theorem of Johnson and Lindenstrauss

metadata.description: Dasgupta-Gupta proves a concentration-of-measure / random-projection result (JL lemma) with no probabilistic-modeling content; Blei-Ng-Jordan defines a hierarchical Bayesian topic model and develops mean-field variational inference for it. The two papers share neither object of study (point clouds in R^d vs document/word multinomials), nor methodology (Gaussian MGF + Markov + union bound vs Dirichlet/multinomial conjugacy + Jensen lower bound + EM), nor target community. Only two extremely soft analogies surface: (i) both invoke a convex-inequality bound on a log/exponential of an expectation (Markov on an exponentiated linear combination vs Jensen on log-marginal), and (ii) both rely on a closed-form moment/log-expectation identity for an exponential-family law (Gaussian MGF vs Dirichlet log-expectation under the digamma function). These are generic toolbox overlaps, not real mathematical correspondences. All paper-original Level-1 contributions on each side have no counterpart on the other side.

matches.explanation: Both proofs apply a convexity-based inequality to bound a log/exponential of an expectation that is otherwise hard to evaluate. Dasgupta-Gupta's PP105.2 (proof of Lemma 2.2(a), step PSP105.5) exponentiates a linear combination of Gaussian squares and applies Markov's inequality to control a tail probability; Blei-Ng-Jordan's PP121.1 (derivation of variational updates, step PSP121.1) multiplies/divides by a variational q inside the integrand of log p(w) and applies Jensen's inequality to obtain the ELBO. The shared move is 'transform the quantity, then push the expectation through a convex function,' but the targets (a tail bound on a sum of chi-square coordinates vs a marginal-likelihood lower bound for a latent-variable model) and the surrounding machinery are unrelated. Listed as a low-confidence analogous match purely to record the methodological echo; it should not be read as a real cross-paper correspondence. Because PP105.2 also appears as the parent of EP105.3 / PSP105.7 (Markov-Chernoff t-optimization) and PP121.1 covers the entire ELBO derivation, this is a deliberately coarse parent-level pairing rather than step-by-step.

Both nodes are closed-form identities for an exponential-family expectation that the rest of the paper plugs in mechanically. EP105.2 is the Gaussian moment generating function E[exp(s X^2)] = (1-2s)^{-1/2}, used to evaluate the exponentiated bound after Markov; PrP121.1 is the Dirichlet log-expectation E[log theta_i] = Psi(alpha_i) - Psi(sum_j alpha_j), used to make the variational lower bound tractable. The analogy is structural ('a textbook identity unlocking the next algebraic step in an exp-family probability calculation') rather than substantive: one is a Gaussian MGF, the other a digamma-based Dirichlet identity, and neither implies the other. Low confidence; recorded for completeness.

The Johnson-Lindenstrauss theorem (existence of a low-distortion linear embedding from R^d into R^k with k = O(log n / eps^2)) is a metric-geometry / random-projection statement. LDA contains no analogue: it does not study Euclidean distance preservation, dimensionality reduction with distortion guarantees, or random projections of point sets.

Lemma 2.2 is a sharp two-sided concentration bound for the squared norm of the projection of a uniform-on-sphere unit vector onto its first k coordinates. LDA never establishes a concentration inequality for any quantity; its probabilistic content is generative modeling and posterior approximation, not tail bounds.

The construction of a uniform random unit vector on S^{d-1} via Gaussian normalization is specific to the random-projection argument. LDA uses Dirichlet- and multinomial-distributed latents; it has no need for a uniform distribution on a sphere.

L = ||Z||^2 with mean k/d (squared length of a coordinate-projected uniform unit vector) is the central random variable of the JL proof. No quantity in LDA plays a comparable role; the LDA latents are categorical (z_n) and simplex-valued (theta), not norms of projected vectors.
An equivalent rewriting of Lemma 2.2(a) in terms of sums of Gaussian squares; purely internal to the JL concentration calculation. No counterpart in LDA.
The optimal Markov-Chernoff parameter t_0 = (1-beta)/(2 beta (d - k beta)) is specific to optimizing the Gaussian-MGF tail bound. LDA performs no such Chernoff optimization.
Elementary log-bounds ln(1-x) <= -x - x^2/2 and ln(1+x) <= x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 used to simplify the JL exponent into eps^2/4 form. LDA does not use these inequalities.

Top-level proof of the JL theorem: random k-subspace + Lemma 2.2 + union bound + rescaling. The proof architecture (concentration on each pair plus union bound over n-choose-2 pairs) has no analogue in LDA's variational/EM derivation.
Symmetric proof of the upper-tail half of Lemma 2.2 (beta > 1). Same conclusion as PP105.2: no LDA counterpart.
'Word' as a one-hot V-vector is a discrete-data primitive specific to text modeling. JL studies arbitrary points in Euclidean space and has no vocabulary/word concept.
'Document' as a sequence of words is a text-modeling primitive with no JL analogue.

'Corpus' as a collection of documents — text-modeling object, no JL counterpart. (One could superficially compare to JL's set V of n points, but the objects, the operations on them, and the goals are unrelated; not a meaningful match.)

The Dirichlet distribution on the (k-1)-simplex is the conjugate prior used throughout LDA. JL's only probabilistic ingredient is the standard multivariate Gaussian (and the induced uniform on S^{d-1}); it never invokes a Dirichlet.

The LDA generative model (Poisson length, Dirichlet topic mixture, multinomial topic and word draws) is the central object of the LDA paper. It has no analogue in JL, which has no generative model whatsoever.
Exchangeability — invariance under permutation of indices — is foundational to LDA's bag-of-words assumption and de Finetti justification. JL has no permutation-invariance content.
Word simplex / topic simplex are geometric objects in the (V-1)-simplex of multinomial parameters. JL works in Euclidean R^d with the L2 norm, not on a probability simplex with a different geometry.
The mean-field variational family q(theta, z | gamma, phi) is specific to LDA's posterior approximation. JL has no posterior to approximate and no variational family.
Smoothed LDA places an exchangeable Dirichlet prior on the topic-word matrix beta. No JL counterpart.
Perplexity as exp(-mean log-likelihood per word) is a language-model evaluation metric. JL has no notion of held-out likelihood or per-token log-probability.
The LDA joint p(theta, z, w | alpha, beta) is the model's defining factorization. No JL analogue.
The marginal document likelihood obtained by integrating out theta and summing out z is specific to the LDA generative model. No JL counterpart.

The intractable LDA posterior is the problem variational inference is built to address. JL solves a different problem (low-distortion embedding existence) and never confronts an intractable posterior.

Minimization of KL(q || p_post) to fit variational parameters has no JL counterpart; JL's only optimization is the parametric Markov-Chernoff t-tuning, which serves a different purpose and uses different machinery.
The closed-form variational coordinate updates for phi and gamma are model-specific to LDA. No JL counterpart.
The M-step closed-form for beta_{ij} (proportional to sum_d sum_n phi*_{dni} w^j_{dn}) is the parameter-estimation update for LDA. No JL counterpart — JL has no learned parameters.
The ELBO decomposition log p(w) = L(gamma, phi; alpha, beta) + KL(q || p_post) is the central variational identity of LDA. JL has no ELBO.
Linear-time Newton-Raphson with rank-one Hessian is a numerical-optimization trick for the alpha M-step. JL performs no Newton-Raphson and has no Hessian.

Coordinate-ascent variational inference for LDA is an algorithm in the EM family. JL contains no EM-style algorithm; its only algorithmic content is the (trivial) randomized projection, which is a single-shot Monte Carlo construction, not an iterative inference procedure.
Variational EM for empirical-Bayes parameter estimation is specific to LDA. No JL counterpart.
Derivation of the M-step closed form for beta via Lagrange multipliers on row-sum constraints — internal to LDA, no JL counterpart.
Newton-Raphson update for the Dirichlet hyperparameter alpha. No JL counterpart.
The posterior-inference problem for LDA has no JL analogue: JL has no Bayesian model and therefore no posterior inference task.
Empirical-Bayes parameter estimation for LDA — a maximum-marginal-likelihood problem. JL is not a learning problem and has no parameters to estimate.
